# The nightly says Chrome and Firefox both passed; our Firefox users disagree

## Problem Description

We ship a storefront. Every night at 02:00 a job runs the end-to-end suite
against a self-hosted browser grid we stand up in CI. Since we set the matrix up
on 2026-06-02 the morning summary has said the same thing every single day:

```
chrome:  41/41 passed
firefox: 41/41 passed
```

On 2026-09-04 we shipped a sticky-header regression that only reproduces in
Firefox — the header eats the first click on the cart button. Support took 63
tickets in two days before anyone connected it to the release. The nightly was
green through all three nights the bug was live, including a night when a manual
tester reproduced it in Firefox on the same build.

Second problem, possibly the same problem, possibly not. Since the 2026-08-21
deploy the nightly sometimes never finishes. It burns the full 45 minutes and
the job gets killed. Roughly one night in four. The pattern I can see from the
partial logs: on every night that hangs there is at least one failing test in
the output before it stops making progress, and on every night that finishes
clean in nine minutes there are none. I widened the grid's session request
timeout to an hour back in August to stop a batch of "session not created"
errors and that did make those go away, so please don't tell me to widen
anything else.

Vlad shelled into the runner on 2026-09-10 while the grid was up and curled the
hub; his saved response is in the files along with everything the job touches.

I want three things: why the Firefox column was lying, how long it has been
lying, and the nightly not hanging any more.

## Output Specification

1. Fix the files in place. Keep the shapes we already use — this repo is not
   getting rewritten this week.
2. `npm test` runs the unit tests on Node's built-in runner and passes today. It
   must still pass, and it must be extended so the reporting problem cannot come
   back unnoticed.
3. Write `docs/nightly-e2e-findings.md`: what the Firefox column actually
   measured, the window during which it measured that, and the mechanism behind
   the hang — each with the line or file you are reading it from.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix the files in place. Keep the shapes we already use — this repo is not
   getting rewritten this week.
2. `npm test` runs the unit tests on Node's built-in runner and passes today. It
   must still pass, and it must be extended so the reporting problem cannot come
   back unnoticed.
3. Write `docs/nightly-e2e-findings.md`: what the Firefox column actually
   measured, the window during which it measured that, and the mechanism behind
   the hang — each with the line or file you are reading it from.
assertions: The three implicated files are edited in place and docs/nightly-e2e-findings.md exists. If `npm test` no longer passes after the edits, this item scores zero.

Taken from the skill's anti-pattern on skipping driver.quit(). endSession must release the session on every path, failure included. Leaving quit behind any condition - the existing flag, a try on the happy path only, a new 'keepOnFailure' option defaulted on - scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require unconditional release plus a stated way to keep the failure evidence the prompt asks for (screenshot or page source captured before the quit). Quitting unconditionally while silently dropping the debugging need, with no mention of it, scores at most half.

The findings document explains the hang as leaked sessions filling the node's slots so later requests sit in the grid's queue, and ties that to the never-reset flag and to the one-hour session request timeout that converted a fast error into a stall. Recommending a longer job timeout, more nodes, or higher max-sessions as the remedy scores zero. Fixing the quit but describing the hang as 'slow tests' or 'flaky grid' scores at most half.

The browser chosen on the command line is what the capabilities request - the argv value is threaded into buildCapabilities (or the workflow and factory are made to agree on one source), so the printed summary and the session can no longer disagree. Correcting only the label or the report file, or adding a matrix entry while leaving the capabilities source untouched, scores zero. Half if the capabilities are fixed but nothing prevents argv and env from drifting apart again.

The firefox node's event-bus settings are corrected so it registers with the hub - publish 4442 and subscribe 4443, matching the chrome node. Leaving the compose file untouched scores zero. Merely noting that the node 'is not registered, check its logs' without correcting the settings scores at most half.

The `sleep 20` step is replaced by polling the hub's status endpoint before the suite runs. Because the saved status shows ready true with only chrome registered, full marks require the check to assert that the browser this job is about is present among the registered slots, not merely that the grid reports ready. Polling readiness alone scores at most half. Keeping or lengthening the sleep scores zero.

A new case in test/ asserts that asking for firefox yields firefox capabilities, and would fail against the factory as shipped. Leaving the test file unchanged scores zero, as does a new test that would also pass against the unfixed factory (for example one that only checks the returned object has a browserName).
The artifact upload is made to run even when the suite step fails, so a failing night still yields its report. Leaving the upload step as shipped scores zero.

The findings document says what the Firefox column was actually measuring and since when, anchored to the 2026-06-02 matrix setup rather than to the September incident. Saying only 'Firefox was not really running' with no window scores at most half.

# The e2e job was green on the release that broke paying for nine hours

## Problem Description

Release 4.11 went out on 2026-09-05 at 08:40. The Place Order button was wired
to a handler that had been renamed, so every checkout attempt in production died
in the browser. We noticed at 17:20 when a customer emailed. Nine hours, no
revenue.

We have had an end-to-end check for exactly that button since March. It lives in
`CheckoutFlow.java` and it is a real test — Petra ran it on her machine against
the 4.11 build and it goes red in four seconds, like it should.

The e2e job on that release commit was green. So was every commit before it in
July and August; I went back through all of them this morning and I cannot find
a red one.

Petra pulled the Maven output from the release build and the list of commits
that have touched the test sources. Both are attached. The artifact the job
uploads from the release build contains exactly one XML file, and it is not for
any of the tests I actually care about.

I need to know why this job reports success while checkout is broken, exactly
how long it has been reporting success without meaning it, and I need it to go
red the next time this happens. I am not interested in adding more tests right
now — I want the ones we already paid for to count.

## Output Specification

1. Edit the build and CI files in place so the next broken checkout turns this
   job red.
2. Do not delete, disable or skip either of the two suites that are not running
   today. If bringing them into the gate requires changing them, change them and
   say what you changed and why.
3. Write `docs/e2e-gate-postmortem.md`: why the job reported success, the exact
   window during which the gate was not gating anything and the change that
   started it, and what specifically to look at on the next run to confirm the
   fix took.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit the build and CI files in place so the next broken checkout turns this
   job red.
2. Do not delete, disable or skip either of the two suites that are not running
   today. If bringing them into the gate requires changing them, change them and
   say what you changed and why.
3. Write `docs/e2e-gate-postmortem.md`: why the job reported success, the exact
   window during which the gate was not gating anything and the change that
   started it, and what specifically to look at on the next run to confirm the
   fix took.
assertions: The build and workflow files are edited in place and docs/e2e-gate-postmortem.md exists. Deleting, disabling or otherwise excluding either of the two non-running suites scores zero for this item, whatever else is done.

The answer identifies that CheckoutFlow and LoginJourney are never picked up because their class names fall outside the test runner's default include patterns, and fixes it - either by renaming them back to names the runner matches, or by configuring explicit includes on the surefire plugin - and says which route it took. Leaving both classes unselected scores zero. Asserting they are 'skipped' or 'disabled' without identifying the selection rule, or changing something that would not actually cause them to run, scores at most half.

`-Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=true` is removed from the CI command and not reintroduced as a plugin property. Leaving it anywhere scores zero. Removing it while ignoring the reason recorded in the comment beside it scores at most half.

The artifact upload step is made to run even when the suite step fails, which is what makes dropping the failure-ignore flag safe. Leaving the upload to be skipped on a failed run scores zero, because the next red build then produces no evidence - the exact reason the flag was added.

From the skill's anti-pattern on a single test class carrying one giant flow: once CheckoutFlow is actually in the gate, its sign-in, browse, add-to-cart, promo and pay steps must be separated into per-behaviour tests with per-test setup, so a red build names the step that broke instead of one method. Leaving the single method intact scores zero. Splitting it into two methods that still bundle unrelated behaviours scores at most half.

The postmortem says what to look at on the next run to confirm the gate is live - an XML report per test class in target/surefire-reports and a per-class run count in the build output, rather than 'the job should fail now'. No verification step at all scores zero; 'just re-run it and see' scores at most half.

Adding continue-on-error, appending `|| true`, passing -DskipTests or -DfailIfNoTests=false, or annotating any test as disabled in order to keep the job passing scores zero for this criterion. The job is allowed - expected - to be red until the application is fixed.

The postmortem dates the loss of coverage to the 2026-04-02 rename commit, not to the September release or to the July commits the requester happened to review. Naming a window without tying it to that commit scores at most half.

# Green on every laptop, red one run in three on the shared runner

## Problem Description

Our browser suite is 11 tests. It passes on every developer machine, every time.
On the shared CI runner it has failed on roughly one run in three since the
middle of July, and it is never the same test twice in a row — last week it was
`test_place_order` on Monday, `test_apply_promo` on Wednesday, and both on
Thursday night.

Two more facts that may or may not belong in the same story:

- Ops has been paging on memory on that runner since 2026-08-02. They sent over
  a process listing they grabbed on 2026-09-08, an hour after a red run. It is
  in the files.
- We cleaned all the fixed waits out of this suite in November last year. Every
  wait in here is an explicit one with a ten-second budget. That was supposed to
  be the end of this class of problem and it clearly wasn't.

I have two changes queued up and about eight hundred pounds a month of runner
budget riding on the second one:

1. Take the explicit wait budget from ten seconds to sixty. The runner is shared
   with two other teams and it is plainly slower than a laptop, so ten seconds
   is probably just too tight for it.
2. Move the job to the 16 GB runner class, since we are paging on memory.

Tell me whether each of those is the right call before I spend anything. If they
are not, I need the actual mechanism for each symptom, not a general tidy-up —
I have to justify this to a finance review on Friday.

Aarti from the front-end team wrote up how the checkout page is put together
after the second failure; her notes are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Edit the test files in place. Do not delete a test.
2. Write `docs/ci-suite-diagnosis.md`. Answer both of my proposed changes
   explicitly and separately — for each one, do it or don't, and the reason —
   and give the mechanism behind each of the two symptoms (the intermittent
   failures, and the memory pressure), citing the file and line you read it
   from.
3. Anything you did not need to change, leave exactly as it is.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit the test files in place. Do not delete a test.
2. Write `docs/ci-suite-diagnosis.md`. Answer both of my proposed changes
   explicitly and separately — for each one, do it or don't, and the reason —
   and give the mechanism behind each of the two symptoms (the intermittent
   failures, and the memory pressure), citing the file and line you read it
   from.
3. Anything you did not need to change, leave exactly as it is.
assertions: The test files are edited in place and docs/ci-suite-diagnosis.md exists and answers the two proposed changes as two separate decisions. Deleting a test scores zero for this item.

The answer must reject the ten-to-sixty-second change and say why it cannot work: the conditions in front of the two failing clicks are satisfied the instant the page paints, because the controls are present and visible while still disabled, so the wait returns at once and the click lands on a disabled control that dispatches nothing. The fix is to wait on a condition that requires the element to be enabled and clickable before clicking. Raising any wait budget, or leaving a presence or visibility condition in front of either gated click, scores zero. Switching to a clickable condition without explaining why sixty seconds would have made no difference scores at most half.

From the skill's anti-pattern on skipping driver.quit(), whose stated consequence is a leaking browser and a CI runner running out of memory. The two tests that construct their own webdriver.Chrome() and call quit() as the final statement of the test body must be changed so the browser is released even when the test fails - the shape the skill uses is creation in setup and quit in teardown. Leaving either quit inside the test body scores zero. Wrapping the body in try/finally inside the test, rather than moving the driver into a fixture, scores at most half.

The diagnosis reads the listing as accumulated orphaned browsers - roughly one per nightly run across 14 days of uptime, 47 of them alive - and therefore rejects the 16 GB runner class as the remedy. Endorsing the larger runner scores zero. Saying only 'browsers are heavy' or 'headless Chrome uses a lot of memory' without engaging with the elapsed times or the count scores at most half.

`time.sleep(3)` in helpers.open_cart is removed in favour of waiting on a condition, and the diagnosis notes that the suite's no-fixed-waits premise was not actually true. Leaving the sleep, shortening it, or moving it elsewhere scores zero. Deleting the line without putting a condition in its place scores at most half.

The session-scoped driver fixture is narrowed so each test gets a fresh browser and a fresh cookie jar, which is also what makes the 'clean session' workaround in test_apply_promo unnecessary. Leaving the fixture at session scope without mentioning it scores zero. Noting the risk but not changing the scope scores at most half.

The diagnosis explains why laptops never see it - the totals request resolves in around 100 ms locally, so the disabled window closes before the click, while a loaded shared runner sometimes loses that race - rather than treating the failures as random flakiness. An answer that offers no account of the laptop-versus-runner difference scores at most half.
MUST NOT modify tests/test_catalog.py. It appears in no failure, uses the fixture correctly and already waits on a clickable condition. Any edit to it scores zero here.

# Two teams, one week, and a consultant who wants us on one tool

## Problem Description

I run platform engineering. The board cut our tooling budget for next year and
asked for a plan to reduce the number of frameworks we pay to train people on.
We brought in a consultant for a fortnight; her memo landed on Monday and it is
attached. Her recommendation is one browser-automation framework across the
whole engineering group, and she has named which one.

Two teams asked me for a decision this week and they are pulling in opposite
directions.

**Atlas** is standing up a brand-new internal admin console. Next.js, TypeScript,
first commit was 2026-08-25, no tests of any kind yet, nothing to migrate, no
compliance surface — it is an internal tool for our own support staff. Their QA
lead wants to write the tests on the same stack Beacon uses, on the grounds that
four of the six people on Atlas already know it and nobody has to learn anything
new. Her exact words were "we would be productive on day one."

**Beacon** is the Rails monolith. Nine years old, it is the product that pays for
everything else. They have about 400 browser specs in Ruby written against
WebDriver, a home-grown reporting service that reads their spec output, and a
government customer whose contract has a clause about how automated test
evidence is produced — the relevant excerpt is attached. Their tech lead read
the memo over the weekend and sent me one line: "are we being asked to port 400
specs, and if so when do we do it?"

I need a recommendation I can forward to both teams on Monday morning, and I
need it to survive being read by the consultant.

One more thing while you are in there. Beacon's invoice-export flow is the thing
that breaks most often — three production incidents this year — and it is still
being tested by hand every release because nobody has had time. The manual
script is attached. Write them the spec for it so Monday's mail has something
concrete in it, and make it look like it belongs in their suite rather than
something dropped in from outside.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/tooling-recommendation.md`: a decision for each team, the reason
   each decision is what it is, and a direct answer to the memo's
   recommendation. Answer Beacon's tech lead's question in the words he asked it.
2. Write `beacon/spec/features/invoice_export_spec.rb` covering the manual
   script, following the conventions of the spec file already in that directory.
3. Do not modify the existing spec file.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/tooling-recommendation.md`: a decision for each team, the reason
   each decision is what it is, and a direct answer to the memo's
   recommendation. Answer Beacon's tech lead's question in the words he asked it.
2. Write `beacon/spec/features/invoice_export_spec.rb` covering the manual
   script, following the conventions of the spec file already in that directory.
3. Do not modify the existing spec file.
assertions: docs/tooling-recommendation.md and beacon/spec/features/invoice_export_spec.rb both exist, and the recommendation gives a separate decision for each team rather than one blended answer. A single recommendation that does not distinguish the two teams scores zero for this item.

The answer must decline the migration and answer the tech lead's question plainly - no, and not later either. Recommending a port, a rewrite, a phased or module-by-module migration, a 'strangler' transition, or a new-specs-on-the-new-tool split for Beacon scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the refusal plus at least two of the three constraints named specifically: the clause that names the protocol the evidence must be produced with, the absence of a first-party client for the language those 400 specs are written in, and the reporting service built on the current output. Declining only because 400 specs is a lot of work, or because 'migrations are risky', scores at most half.

Atlas is directed to a modern framework rather than to Beacon's stack, and the answer says why familiarity is not a reason to carry an older stack onto a greenfield project with nothing to migrate and no compliance surface. Recommending the incumbent stack for Atlas scores zero. Declaring the choice a toss-up, or deferring it to the team, scores at most half.

The recommendation addresses the memo's two load-bearing claims directly: that the named framework supports every language in use, and that it is standards-based so contractual commitments are unaffected. Repeating either claim as fact, or writing a recommendation that never engages with the memo, scores zero. Disputing one of the two scores at most half.

From the skill's anti-pattern on skipping driver.quit(): the new spec must quit the driver in an after hook, as the neighbouring spec file does, so a failing example does not strand a browser. No quit, a quit only on the success path, or a quit placed at the end of the example body scores zero for this criterion.

Export and Download are described in the manual script as unavailable until the count settles and until the status reads Ready, and the spec waits for those conditions rather than sleeping or clicking blind. Any fixed sleep in the new spec scores zero. Waiting for mere presence of a control the script says starts disabled or absent scores at most half.

It reuses the helpers and setup shape already in spec_helper.rb - the driver builder, the sign-in helper, the wait - and uses the data-testid selectors the manual script names. Inventing a parallel setup, a second driver builder or a different selector convention scores at most half.

The recommendation states what keeping two stacks costs and why that cost is worth paying here, rather than ignoring the budget question that prompted the review. An answer that never addresses the consolidation goal scores at most half.
MUST NOT modify beacon/spec/features/checkout_spec.rb. It passes, it is the reference for the new file's conventions, and it was not part of the request. Any edit to it scores zero here.

# The payment specs break every time the card vendor ships, and now six agents won't start a browser

## Problem Description

Our checkout embeds a hosted card-entry component from a payments vendor. It
renders into our own DOM — it is not in an iframe — and the vendor ships a new
build roughly monthly with no notice and no changelog we can subscribe to.

Our payment specs have broken four times since June: 2026-06-18, 2026-07-09,
2026-08-11 and 2026-09-03. Every one of those was within a few hours of a vendor
release, every one was a locator that stopped resolving, and every one cost
someone half a day. Nobody trusts the payment specs any more; on 2026-08-11 the
on-call engineer assumed it was the vendor again and it was actually us.

The constraint I cannot move: **that markup is not ours.** We cannot add
attributes to it, we do not build it, and the vendor's support desk has an
eleven-day median response. Whatever we do has to work against markup we do not
control.

Marina saved the rendered component from the build that was live in June and
from the one live now, both straight out of the browser. They are attached. I
would like the next vendor build to be a non-event.

Separate but urgent: the build agents took a Chrome update on 2026-09-08 and six
of the eleven now fail before a single test runs. The stack trace from
`build-agent-07` is attached. Right now the release is going out on five agents
and everything is queued behind them.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite the locators in `PaymentPage.java` so that a vendor build of the kind
   visible between those two snapshots does not break them.
2. Fix whatever is stopping six agents from starting a browser, in the files
   provided.
3. Write `docs/vendor-widget-locators.md`: for each control on that component,
   the hook you chose and the evidence from the two snapshots that it is a
   durable one. Say plainly which controls have no durable hook of their own and
   what you did about them.
4. Leave `LoginTest.java` alone — it passes and it is not part of this.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite the locators in `PaymentPage.java` so that a vendor build of the kind
   visible between those two snapshots does not break them.
2. Fix whatever is stopping six agents from starting a browser, in the files
   provided.
3. Write `docs/vendor-widget-locators.md`: for each control on that component,
   the hook you chose and the evidence from the two snapshots that it is a
   durable one. Say plainly which controls have no durable hook of their own and

assertions: PaymentPage.java is rewritten, the agent failure is addressed in the provided files, and docs/vendor-widget-locators.md exists with a per-control entry. A document that gives general locator advice without naming the six controls on this component scores zero for this item.

Card number, expiry, the pay button and the error element are located by hooks that are identical in both snapshots - the name or autocomplete or aria-label attributes, the submit type, the alert role - rather than by anything that changed. Any hashed class name surviving in PaymentPage.java scores zero for this criterion, as does any absolute or index-based path. Using the element ids scores zero: both ids differ between the two snapshots. A locator that merely happens to match the current snapshot without evidence of stability scores at most half.

The CVC input and the save-card checkbox are located relative to something durable - the visible label text beside them, via a relationship query or a relative locator anchored on a stable element. Locating either by a hashed class, by sibling index, or by a bare input[type=checkbox] that the second snapshot already shows is ambiguous scores zero. Locating them by an attribute that is present in only one of the two snapshots, such as the CVC field's maxlength, scores at most half.

From the skill's anti-pattern on a hardcoded ChromeDriver path: the pinned webdriver.chrome.driver system property must go, replaced by driver resolution that tracks the installed browser - either the resolver bundled with this version of the library or an explicit driver-manager dependency. Repointing the property at a newer binary, adding a version constant, or pinning the browser version on the agents instead scores zero. Removing the property without saying what now resolves the driver scores at most half.

The document states which attributes survived the vendor build and which did not, naming at least the hashed classes, the ids and the added wrapper depth as the things that changed. Asserting a hook is stable with no reference to the two snapshots scores at most half; getting the direction wrong - for example calling the ids stable - scores zero.

The answer connects the six failing agents to the Chrome update and the five passing ones to the group policy pin, and says that the surviving five are passing for a reason that will expire rather than because they are configured correctly. Treating the five as the desired state scores zero.

Given an eleven-day median response and markup the team does not build, asking the vendor to add test attributes cannot be the remedy. Making it the plan, or delivering a locator strategy that only works once the vendor acts, scores zero. Raising it as a separate longer-term request alongside a strategy that works against today's markup is fine and costs nothing here.
